name: Tria Positively Clear

card.summary: A hand-held at-home blue light device from Tria Beauty, cleared by the FDA for mild to moderate inflammatory acne, used to help clear breakouts and even out skin.
card.note: Not intended for nodular or cystic acne per retailer guidance; efficacy claims come largely from the manufacturer.

quick.overview:
Positively Clear is a hand-held blue light device from Tria Beauty that users hold against the skin for short daily sessions. Blue light is described as acting on acne-causing bacteria, so the aim is fewer inflamed breakouts and clearer-looking skin.

The company announced over-the-counter FDA clearance in January 2010 for mild to moderate inflammatory acne. The company reports clinical studies showing results comparable to professional blue light treatment; those studies are described in company materials rather than detailed publications.
quick.how: Users press the device to a section of skin for a short timed treatment, with the company's study description citing two to three minutes twice a day and retail listings describing a roughly five-minute daily session. It is used alongside a normal skincare routine.
quick.risks: Retailer guidance warns against use on nodular or cystic acne. Dermatology references describe blue light as having an unclear benefit and as an add-on rather than a first-line acne treatment.

lead: Tria Positively Clear is a hand-held blue light acne device sold by Tria Beauty, the company behind the Tria laser hair removal system. It is meant for home use to help clear mild to moderate inflammatory acne, with the benefit of calmer, clearer skin.[1]

Tria announced FDA over-the-counter clearance on 9 January 2010. The company describes the blue light as killing acne-causing bacteria and as delivering an effective dose in shorter treatment times; it states the light is ten times more powerful than other over-the-counter blue light devices.[1]

Company-reported studies used the device for two to three minutes, twice a day, and the company says breakouts cleared as quickly as with professional blue light and a leading prescription drug. The announcement does not give sample sizes or publication details.[1] General dermatology references describe blue light therapy as of unclear benefit and as an add-on option.[2]

angle.text: Users apply the light to breakout-prone areas in short sessions to reduce inflammatory acne. The manufacturer positions it as an at-home alternative to office blue light treatments.

infobox: About 2 to 5 minutes (company and retailer descriptions)

paras: The device is a hand-held blue light unit built by the scientists who designed the Tria laser hair removal system. The company markets it as the base of a system for clearer skin.[1]
Tria announced over-the-counter clearance from the US FDA in January 2010 for treating mild to moderate inflammatory acne.[1]

Tria reports multiple clinical studies by dermatologists, with two to three minute sessions twice daily, finding speed of clearing comparable to professional blue light and a leading prescription drug; no sample sizes, designs or publications are given in the announcement, and these are company statements.[1] Broader reviews of blue light for acne describe its benefit as unclear.[2]
Retail listings describe a daily treatment of about five minutes and advise against using it on nodular or cystic acne.

timeline.event: Tria Beauty announces OTC FDA clearance for its hand-held blue light device.[1]
